intro: The elephant sanctuaries and conservation centres where you can meet elephants with a clear conscience — feeding, bathing and walking with them and learning mahout life, rather than shows or rides. Most are in the north (Chiang Mai, Lampang) and in Surin, Thailand's real elephant country, each with the best time to go and where to stay.

blocks.html: Short answer: For an easy first visit choose a Chiang Mai sanctuary built around feeding and bathing, no riding; for serious conservation and an elephant hospital, the Thai Elephant Conservation Center in Lampang; for mahout culture and the most domesticated elephants in the country, Ban Ta Klang Elephant Village (Surin); and to see hundreds of elephants at once, the Surin Elephant Round-up in mid-November. The tip: pick places with no riding or bullhooks, and go on a cool morning when the elephants are at their happiest.

items.name: Ethical Elephant Sanctuaries (Chiang Mai)
items.blurb: Chiang Mai is the easiest place in Thailand to find a no-riding, no-show sanctuary, where many camps let you hand-feed bananas, join a mud bath and simply walk with the herd through the hills. Check that a place uses no riding or bullhooks before you book, pick a half-day program if you have kids, and go on the cool morning slot.

items.name: Thai Elephant Conservation Center (Lampang)
items.blurb: A government centre at Hang Chat doing real conservation work, with an elephant hospital that treats sick elephants from across the country and a mahout training school. You can look in on retired and injured elephants being cared for, visit the hospital free and leave a donation, and it sits handily between Chiang Mai and Lampang.

items.name: Ban Ta Klang Elephant Village (Surin)
items.blurb: The largest domesticated-elephant village in the country, home to the Kui people who have treated elephants like family for generations, with an Elephant Study Center and museum that explain real mahout life. The centre helps keep almost 200 mahouts and their elephants at home instead of roaming the cities; it's open year-round, and early mornings you'll catch the elephants bathing in the river.

items.name: Surin Elephant Round-up
items.blurb: An annual festival in mid-November that gathers hundreds of elephants from across Surin in one place — a cultural heritage of Thailand's elephant heartland, held every year since 1960. In 2026 it falls on 19–21 November; it draws big crowds and rooms fill up early, so book ahead and reach the stadium early for a good seat.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit an elephant sanctuary?
faq.a: Sanctuaries and conservation centres like Chiang Mai and Lampang are open year-round, so any season works, but the cool months (Nov–Feb) are the most comfortable for walking with the elephants. Morning slots usually beat afternoons — gentler sun and happier elephants — while the Surin Round-up runs once a year in mid-November (19–21 Nov in 2026).

faq.q: Can I bring kids to an elephant sanctuary?
faq.a: Yes — kids usually love the banana-feeding and bathing parts, but pick a place with no riding and mahouts staying close. A half-day program suits young children, and always keep kids within the distance the mahout tells you, since elephants are big and move faster than you'd expect.

faq.q: How much does it cost, and how do I get there?
faq.a: Most private Chiang Mai sanctuaries sell half- or full-day packages that include hotel pickup and lunch, with prices depending on the program, while the Thai Elephant Conservation Center in Lampang charges a modest entry fee and lets you visit the elephant hospital for free. Ban Ta Klang in Surin is in Tha Tum district, about an hour from the city, and is easiest with your own car or a hired one.
